examTakeaway: A physician who is impaired while caring for patients must be stopped that day, while a remote treated illness with current fitness does not.
scenario: A 50-year-old surgeon and a 52-year-old surgeon are discussed at noon. One smells of alcohol and is about to operate. The other had a treated substance problem five years ago, is in monitoring, and has a normal exam today. Both have full privileges on paper.
question: Which surgeon has to be stopped before the next case?
options: The one in monitoring with a normal exam today
Both, because any history is current impairment
Neither, because privileges are already granted
Only the monitored surgeon, because paperwork replaces an exam
The one who smells of alcohol and is about to operate
correctAnswer: The one who smells of alcohol and is about to operate
explanation: A physician who is impaired while caring for patients must be stopped that day, while a remote treated illness with current fitness does not. The one who smells of alcohol and is about to operate is the surgeon to stop. The one in monitoring with a normal exam today is fit to work. Both, because any history is current impairment, erases recovery. Neither, because privileges are already granted, leaves an impaired operator in the room. Only the monitored surgeon, because paperwork replaces an exam, punishes the well surgeon.

examTakeaway: A minor's visit for a sexually transmitted infection stays confidential, while a request for a body piercing does not.
scenario: A 16-year-old girl has two requests. She wants treatment for a vaginal discharge and asks that her parents not be told. She also wants a note approving a tongue piercing and asks that this also be secret. She is not pregnant. She can describe both requests.
question: Which request can stay confidential?
options: Both
Neither, because she is 16
The piercing note, because it is the smaller request
Treatment of the infection
The piercing note
correctAnswer: Treatment of the infection
explanation: A minor's visit for a sexually transmitted infection stays confidential, while a request for a body piercing does not. Treatment of the infection can stay confidential. The piercing note needs a parent. Both flattens a protected service and a cosmetic request. Neither, because she is 16, ignores the infection exception. The piercing note, because it is the smaller request, protects the wrong one.

examTakeaway: An unexpected death in the emergency department is a medical-examiner case, while an expected hospice death is not.
scenario: Two deaths occur on the same night. One is a 40-year-old man who collapsed in the emergency department and never had a diagnosis. The other is an 80-year-old woman on hospice who died of a cancer the team has followed for months. Families of both ask that nobody official be called.

options: The hospice death, because cancer is always examined
The unexplained emergency-department death
The expected hospice death
Both
Neither, because the families objected
correctAnswer: The unexplained emergency-department death
explanation: An unexpected death in the emergency department is a medical-examiner case, while an expected hospice death is not. The unexplained emergency-department death is reported. The expected hospice death is not. Both over-reports a known expected death. Neither, because the families objected, lets a family cancel a legal duty. The hospice death, because cancer is always examined, reverses the cases.

examTakeaway: Consent for surgery needs a professional interpreter, and an adult child who offers to translate is the wrong person for that conversation.
scenario: A 68-year-old woman speaks only Spanish. Her adult son offers to interpret the consent for a colectomy. A professional interpreter is available by video within minutes. The son says he already told her it is a small operation. She looks uncertain.
question: Why is the son the wrong interpreter for this consent?
options: A family member is always the best interpreter
Video interpretation is less accurate than a relative
Consent does not require understanding the operation
The son may interpret because he is an adult
He may soften, omit, or decide for her
correctAnswer: He may soften, omit, or decide for her
explanation: Consent for surgery needs a professional interpreter, and an adult child who offers to translate is the wrong person for that conversation. He may soften, omit, or decide for her, which he has already begun to do. A family member is always the best interpreter is the offer being refused. Video interpretation is less accurate than a relative is not a reason to skip a professional. Consent does not require understanding the operation is false. The son may interpret because he is an adult confuses his age with her informed choice.

examTakeaway: A capacitated patient may leave against advice, while a delirious patient who tries to walk out does not get that choice.
scenario: A 60-year-old patient and a 62-year-old patient want to walk out. One has pneumonia, understands the risk of death, repeats it, and is not confused. The other is febrile, pulling at lines, and cannot say where he is. Both are angry. Security is in the hall.

options: Neither, because the physician disagrees
The delirious patient, because he is more insistent
The one who can repeat the risk and is not confused
The delirious patient
Both, because anger is capacity
correctAnswer: The one who can repeat the risk and is not confused
explanation: A capacitated patient may leave against advice, while a delirious patient who tries to walk out does not get that choice. The one who can repeat the risk and is not confused may leave. The delirious patient is kept safely. Both, because anger is capacity, confuses emotion with the abilities. Neither, because the physician disagrees, traps a capacitated patient. The delirious patient, because he is more insistent, rewards the inability to decide.

examTakeaway: A donor designation on the license stands over a family's objection after death.
scenario: A 30-year-old man is brain dead. His license documents a choice to donate organs. His parents demand that donation stop. There is no later writing that revokes the license. The organs are still suitable.

The parents, if they are distressed

explanation: A donor designation on the license stands over a family's objection after death. The documented choice on the license stands. examTakeaway: A clinician does not date a current patient, while a relationship with someone who was never a patient is not that boundary.
scenario: Two invitations arrive. A current patient asks the physician to dinner and has a follow-up visit next week. A neighbor who has never been a patient asks the same physician to dinner. The physician is unmarried and not caring for the neighbor's family.

Dinner with the current patient

examTakeaway: Leftover blood that still carries a name needs consent for a new study, while a fully deidentified leftover sample can be used under a waiver.
scenario: A lab holds two saved tubes from a 50-year-old patient. One is labeled with a name, a date of birth, and a medical record number. The other was stripped of every identifier before it was stored, and no code remains. A researcher wants both for a new question the patients never heard.

examTakeaway: A case that includes the date and a rare disease in a small town identifies the patient, even with the name removed.
scenario: A resident wants to post two stories about a patient. One says a middle-aged adult had a common pneumonia in a large city, with no dates and no other details. The other gives the date, the town of 2,000 people, and a rare tumor. Neither uses a name.

The common pneumonia with no dates

examTakeaway: When a patient names a surrogate and loses capacity, that person speaks, not the relative who arrives later and disagrees.

examTakeaway: A near miss that never reached the patient is reported inside the system, and the patient is not given a frightening non-event as if it injured him.

examTakeaway: A trainee does not do a procedure for the first time on a patient without telling the patient who will be doing it and who will be supervising.

examTakeaway: A thiazide lowers urine calcium, so it is the wrong diuretic when the serum calcium is already high.

examTakeaway: Low magnesium keeps potassium channels open in the distal nephron, so potassium replacement fails until magnesium is replaced.

A normal creatinine means the kidney cannot waste potassium

Magnesium must be replaced or the kidney keeps wasting potassium

examTakeaway: Blood at the urethral meatus after a pelvic injury means a urethral tear until proven otherwise, so a Foley catheter is the wrong first tube.

examTakeaway: A clenched fist or a long delay can leak potassium from cells in the tube, so a potassium of 7 with a normal ECG is repeated before it is treated as real.

examTakeaway: Erythropoietin cannot build red cells without iron, so a shot is wasted when ferritin is empty.
